Family Health

Bleeding with the contraceptive injection: what can help?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Bleeding changes are common with the contraceptive injection. You can ask for help before the next dose, whether the concern is heavy bleeding, unpredictable spotting or a method that no longer suits your life.

How the injection changes pregnancy risk and bleeding

Depo-Provera contains depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, or DMPA, a long-acting progestogen. It is related to the body’s progesterone but is not the same hormone. Its main contraceptive effect is to suppress ovulation; it also alters cervical mucus and the lining of the uterus.

The mucus makes sperm passage more difficult, while changes in the uterine lining help explain why bleeding no longer follows the same pattern as an untreated menstrual cycle. A simple story about a fertilised egg being unable to attach is not the best explanation of its principal contraceptive action.

Regular injections provide highly effective contraception, but pregnancy risk is not zero. The CDC estimates about four pregnancies per hundred users in the first year with typical use, which includes delays and missed doses. Bleeding is not a test of how well the method is working.

Spotting and irregular bleeding are common early on

You may notice light spotting, bleeding between expected periods or an unpredictable pattern after the first injection. It can continue for several months. Some people find that it becomes less frequent, while others remain bothered by it.

Figures depend on how a study defines bleeding and when it measures it. An often-quoted single percentage for the whole first year should not be treated as a personal prediction. The important question is whether your bleeding is manageable and whether another cause needs checking.

There is no guaranteed point at six months, twelve months or after the third or fourth injection when every symptom will stop. Arrange a review if the pattern is affecting your life rather than waiting for a promised adjustment date.

Heavier or longer bleeding still deserves attention

A longer or heavier episode can occur, but it should not automatically be attributed to DMPA. Tell the service about the amount, duration, clots, pain and any change after a previously stable pattern.

Do not wait until fourteen continuous days have passed before asking for help. Earlier assessment is appropriate when bleeding is heavy, painful, persistent or troubling. Unusual tiredness, breathlessness or lightheadedness may prompt a check for anaemia as well as investigation of the bleeding.

Very heavy bleeding with faintness, severe abdominal pain, fever or feeling seriously unwell needs urgent care. A possible pregnancy with one-sided pain or shoulder-tip pain also needs prompt assessment.

Lighter periods or no periods can be an expected effect

Periods often become lighter or stop with continued use. The US prescribing information reports no periods in 55 percent of users at twelve months in its clinical studies. That is a study result, not a guarantee for an individual or a reason to compare yourself with another user.

The absence of bleeding, called amenorrhoea, usually does not need treatment while using DMPA. It does not mean menstrual blood is trapped inside the uterus.

Pregnancy testing can still be appropriate if an injection was late, symptoms suggest pregnancy or the pattern changes unexpectedly. Do not use either spotting or absent periods as proof of continued contraceptive protection.

Other symptoms are worth discussing too

Reported symptoms include abdominal discomfort, changes in weight or appetite, headache, nausea, dizziness and breast pain or tenderness. Mood changes, reduced sexual desire, fatigue or weakness may also be reported.

Skin and hair concerns can include acne, hair loss or increased facial or body hair. A symptom that appears during use may be related to the medicine, another condition or several factors. Reports in a product leaflet do not establish the cause in your case.

It is inaccurate to say that all non-bleeding effects are rare, mild or certain to settle. Describe new or persistent symptoms, including significant mood changes, before deciding whether to continue. Sudden severe headache, weakness, vision loss, chest pain or breathlessness needs urgent assessment.

The injection cannot be removed, but symptoms can be treated

DMPA is designed to release medicine over time. Once it has been injected, it cannot be taken out in the way an implant can be removed. Stopping means not receiving further doses and planning what happens next.

That does not mean you must wait without help. The clinician can assess the bleeding, consider short-term treatment and discuss a different contraceptive method. Avoid attempts to flush out the hormone or reverse it with supplements.

Improvement may occur as use continues, but the body does not follow a fixed learning schedule. Your preference matters even if the bleeding is judged medically harmless.

Check for other causes before choosing a treatment

Bring the date of the last injection, a record of bleeding, pregnancy-test results and a list of medicines and supplements. Mention pelvic pain, discharge, a new sexual-health concern or any late doses.

Depending on the findings, assessment may include pregnancy or STI testing, an examination, a blood count or investigation for conditions such as thyroid disease, polyps or fibroids. Not everyone needs every test.

Ask whether the proposed treatment is intended to reduce the present bleeding, treat another diagnosis or change contraception. Those are related but different decisions.

Short courses of medicine may help

For suitable patients, a clinician may consider a short course of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or NSAID, such as an appropriate ibuprofen regimen. CDC guidance describes five to seven days as an option during bleeding. It does not provide a universal self-treatment dose.

For heavy or prolonged bleeding, a low-dose combined pill or oestrogen may sometimes be considered for a short course if medically appropriate. Evidence for particular regimens is limited, and bleeding may return after treatment. The advice is more nuanced than either nothing works or extra oestrogen will reliably repair the lining.

Kidney disease, stomach ulcers, medicine interactions and other factors can make an NSAID unsuitable. Added oestrogen has separate risks and contraindications. Do not borrow hormone tablets or increase ibuprofen yourself; ask about the intended benefit, duration and follow-up.

Keep the next injection date separate from the bleeding pattern

Injections are usually scheduled about every twelve to thirteen weeks, depending on the product and local instructions. The CDC uses thirteen weeks for US DMPA guidance, while some product schedules differ. Follow the appointment date given by your service.

If you are late, contact the service promptly and use condoms or avoid sex until you have a clear protection and restart plan. Grace periods are not identical everywhere, so an automatic rule that one week late means the same thing for every product is unreliable.

Tell the clinician about unprotected sex, particularly in the previous five days, because emergency contraception may be relevant. The choice and timing must fit the restart plan; a pregnancy test taken too soon after sex can miss a pregnancy. The injection does not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

Medical history and medicine interactions affect suitability

Before the next dose, discuss current or previous breast cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, liver disease, clotting history, pregnancy possibility and any other important health condition. The clinician should use the current local product information and eligibility guidance.

Bring every medicine and supplement. The UK product information specifically flags aminoglutethimide because it can reduce the amount of DMPA available in the body. This requires a medicine review; do not stop a prescribed treatment on your own.

Wanting to conceive soon is a planning issue rather than an automatic medical contraindication. Another method may fit that aim better because return of fertility after DMPA can be delayed.

Bone health and meningioma warnings need context

DMPA can reduce bone mineral density. A history of fragility fractures, other bone-health risks and planned duration of use should be reviewed. A past fracture alone is not enough for this article to declare that someone can never use the method.

The US label advises against long-term use beyond two years unless other options are considered inadequate; local recommendations require an individual discussion of benefits and risks. Do not apply a different country’s label as an unexplained rule for your prescription.

Current product information also includes a meningioma warning, particularly relevant to prolonged exposure. A meningioma is a tumour of the membranes around the brain or spinal cord, usually non-cancerous. Tell the prescriber about any current or previous diagnosis and report new progressive neurological symptoms. This information supports a review, not a prediction that an individual will develop a tumour.

Plan for continuing, switching or trying for pregnancy

Effects on bleeding can last beyond the nominal injection interval and may continue for weeks or months after stopping. Periods and ovulation do not necessarily return together on a fixed date. A delayed return does not by itself mean permanent infertility.

If you do not want pregnancy, arrange another method before protection ends. Ongoing spotting or the absence of a period cannot tell you that the previous injection is still preventing ovulation.

If you want to continue, discuss the bleeding and any treatment before the next dose. If you want to change methods, say so. Convenience and effectiveness are benefits, but satisfaction is personal and should not be promised simply because you have waited long enough.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bleeding changes may be expected, but other causes should be considered when indicated.

Short-term treatment is sometimes appropriate after checking medical suitability and preferences.

How BeMama can help

Keep injection dates and a brief bleeding record together. At review, explain whether you want to continue with support, change methods or plan a pregnancy.

When to seek help

Very heavy bleeding, faintness, severe pain or major new neurological, chest or breathing symptoms needs urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • No bleeding pattern proves that contraception is still effective.
  • There is no guaranteed date when all side effects settle.
  • A given injection cannot be removed, but symptom treatment may be possible.
  • Check the schedule and missed-dose advice for your own product and country.
  • Continuing or switching is a shared decision based on your needs.

Frequently asked questions

Does spotting mean Depo-Provera has stopped working?

Not by itself. Protection depends on correct use and timing, not the bleeding pattern.

Will every user have no periods after a year?

No. Many do, but the pattern varies and study percentages do not predict an individual result.

Is blood building up if I do not bleed?

Usually no; absent bleeding is an expected effect of the changed uterine lining. Pregnancy testing may still be appropriate in some circumstances.

Must I wait fourteen days before calling about bleeding?

No. Ask earlier if it is heavy, painful, persistent or affecting daily life.

Can the injection be removed once it has been given?

No, but the clinician can assess symptoms and discuss treatment or future contraception.

Can I use a high dose of ibuprofen to stop the bleeding?

Do not self-prescribe a bleeding regimen. Suitability, dose and duration need individual advice.

Is extra oestrogen suitable for everyone?

No. It has separate risks and contraindications, and its benefit may be temporary.

What should I do if I am late for an injection?

Contact the service promptly, use backup until advised and report recent unprotected sex so emergency contraception and testing can be considered.

Does a previous fracture automatically rule out DMPA?

No single fact settles suitability. The prescriber should assess the type of fracture, other bone risks and alternatives.

Do absent periods after stopping mean I cannot become pregnant?

No. Fertility can return unpredictably, and the delay is not proof of permanent infertility or continuing protection.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
